key_insight: Most of the LLM-generated clinical corpus was not new information: only 10.9% was trainable-unique content, while 79.4% was redundant.
clinical_relevance: For clinical NLP training data, raw token counts can greatly overstate usable information, so deduplication and provenance-aware curation can improve model adaptation efficiency.
method: Analyzed the full output of a multi-agent clinical extraction pipeline on 167,034 patient narratives.
Classified 2.51 billion generated tokens by source using Provenance-based Redundancy Decomposition.
Validated redundancy patterns with lossless compression, independent of provenance labels.
evidence_signal: A downstream controlled test showed that de-duplicating the corpus before adaptation improved a clinical encoder on external disease-recognition benchmarks at equal token budget, and the result replicated on a second benchmark.
watch_item: Some redundancy is only losslessly removable when it comes from copied source context; duplicated generated text across records may require more careful handling to avoid altering content distribution.
paper_title: How much of an LLM-generated clinical corpus is actually new? A production-scale measurement of content redundancy for provenance classification
